# Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite

Jonno,

You can stop messaging me about the coolroom now. This is the whole story. I’m putting it here because if I type it out to you on my phone after another double I’m going to lose the use of a thumb, and then you’ll have to come back from London and do some actual work.

Actually, you’d have been no use. London’s made you soft. You’ve been there since February and I reckon by now you’d need a little sit-down if someone double-docketed the grill.

You would’ve fucking cried on Cup Day.

At 6.40 on Tuesday morning I looked at the coolroom thermometer and it said 11 degrees.

Eleven.

I stood there looking at it for a bit, which didn’t help. Checked it again, which also didn’t help. The compressor had died overnight, sometime between Monday and Tuesday, because apparently it had looked at the bookings and decided it wasn’t interested.

We had 140 covers booked for lunch. Set menu. Three courses. Raff was away, so I was running it.

You know when you get in early because you want a nice quiet hour to get ahead? Anyway.

Rang Wally from Coldline. Wally couldn’t get there until Wednesday. Part had to come from Sydney. I don’t blame Wally, but I did briefly hate Sydney. Nothing personal against anyone there. Just seemed a stupid place to keep the particular thing I needed in Melbourne.

Phil gave me “just make it work mate”.

Cheers Phil. Hadn’t thought of that. I was going to put my apron back in my bag and go stand in the middle of the road, but now that you’ve outlined the plan I can crack on.

“Just make it work mate” is not a plan. It’s what an owner says when he’d like the conversation to be finished but the restaurant to remain open.

So we started sorting through it all. Worked out what had to go, what we could save, and where the fuck we were going to put everything. Both undercounters. The bar fridge. Then Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which is the reason this is a blog post about a lunch service and not a post announcing that I’ve left hospitality to do something with spreadsheets.

We lost about $1,800 in stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs.

I haven’t got a funny bit for the duck legs. Still annoyed about those.

The rest of the morning involved finding out how much of a restaurant you can fit inside several much smaller fridges. Not as much as you’d like. More than seems reasonable. Every time somebody needed something, someone else had to explain which building it was in.

You’d have hated that. You used to get the shits if the butter moved six inches.

At one point Benny and I had 30 kilos of beef shin on a milk crate trolley, taking it down the laneway in the rain to Marta’s.

Then a wheel fell off.

Not a little wobble. Not a warning noise that gave us a chance to stop and think, that wheel looks a bit ordinary. Just off. Finished. Another piece of equipment declining to participate in Melbourne Cup Day.

Thirty kilos of beef shin is a fair bit of beef shin when you’re suddenly down a wheel.

I thought of you then. Not because I missed you. Because I knew exactly the face you would’ve pulled, and because you would’ve stood there telling us the trolley was fucked while we were quite clearly experiencing that information.

Benny and I got it there. Wet, furious, still with a lunch service to do.

Meanwhile Kev had gone to the servo for ice. Fourteen bags, into the old esky.

The bloke at the servo asked if we were having a party.

I hope Kev said yes. Technically we were. Big lunch, everyone dressed up, plenty of drinks. Just a slightly different experience out the back, where the catering staff were distributing ice and checking what else had broken.

By then the kitchen was operating across two undercounters, a bar fridge, an esky and another business. If you’d walked in without knowing what was happening you might have thought we were closing down very slowly.

And then lunch started.

That was the bit I’d been dreading, obviously. Up until then you can keep moving things and swearing and ringing people. Once the tickets start, you still have all those problems, except now someone wants their entree.

But everyone was properly on.

Benny, Kev, the whole crew. No one needed the big speech. No one had time for one, either. Everyone knew we were in the shit and just got on with their bit. If something needed doing, somebody did it.

You know those services where you spend half your time asking for something you should already have? It wasn’t one of those. Which was handy, because what we should already have had was a functioning coolroom.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

That’s not me doing charming blog language. That was pretty much where we were at. Affogato, plus whatever we could manage.

People loved it.

Possibly more than they would’ve loved the panna cotta, which I’m trying not to take personally on behalf of every panna cotta I’ve ever made. All that planning and prep and apparently the thing people actually want is coffee tipped over ice cream.

Fair enough. So do I, most days.

A lady on table nine had seen Benny and me out the window with the beef. Asked if it was “free range from the laneway”.

Good gear. Can’t fault her. We’d given her plenty to work with.

I’d rather that than someone asking whether we were having a party.

And somehow, after all of it, I reckon it was the best service we’ve done all year.

Don’t get excited. I’m not saying we should break the fridge before Christmas to build team spirit. I’d quite happily have done a slightly worse service with all our stock intact and dry socks.

But it was good. Really good. Everyone was locked in, the food went out, people enjoyed their lunch. There’s a particular sort of satisfaction in getting through one like that, even if you only get about three seconds to appreciate it before you remember the mess.

Marta is getting paid back in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. Whatever she wants, honestly. Half a walk-in on Cup Day buys you a lot of goodwill and the right to bring this up whenever you need a favour.

I also had a horse in the sweep.

Ice Cold Lad.

Second last.

I don’t follow racing closely enough to know whether that counts as form, but it felt consistent with everything else bearing any relation to refrigeration that day. The universe is taking the piss.

So that’s what happened. You saw thirty seconds of it on my story and have spent the week asking questions like there’s a formal incident report coming. Here you go. Compressor dead, duck gone, trolley fucked, lunch somehow excellent.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. Also Kev, apparently, and the generosity of the cafe next door.

You would’ve lost your mind. You’d have complained the whole way down the laneway, then spent the rest of service doing twice as much work as anyone asked you to. I’ll give you that.

Would’ve been good to have you there.

Come home ya flog.
